Between opposite corners there are two equally short routes, such as 1, 2, 3 (accent color) and 1, 4, 3 (teal). The matrix counts the shortest paths for every source and target: 2 for the four opposite pairs (highlighted) and 1 otherwise, 20 paths in total." width="100%"} Runs `single_source_all_shortest_paths()` from every node. The output can be very large, since the number of shortest paths grows quickly with graph size; it is meant for small graphs, teaching, and exhaustive checks. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, dict[int, list[list[int]]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `result[source][target]` is the sorted list of shortest paths. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a negative cycle exists. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} One predecessor search per source plus path enumeration; matches NetworkX's `all_pairs_all_shortest_paths`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#0a811741 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec square = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(4) everything = square.all_pairs_all_shortest_paths() sum(len(paths) for row in everything.values() for paths in row.values()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 20 ``` ::: :::
